species.name: Red drum
species.local: redfish, spottail bass, spottail; adults over the slot are bull reds
species.present: Year-round. Juveniles and slot fish stay in the creeks and marsh. Adults spend most of the year offshore and come into the sounds and inlets in late summer and fall to spawn (SCDNR).
species.peak: Tailing on flood tides from mid-March to the end of November (local guide). Bull reds from late August to November in the sounds, inlets and surf. SCDNR puts spawning in a short window in August and September. Hilton Head captains call October the best inshore month for bulls, and the Hunting Island surf runs September to November. In the May River, Beaufort County, red drum call most in September and October (USC Beaufort recordings). In winter they school on low-tide mud flats in clear water.
species.where: Slot fish: spartina flats, oyster bars, creek mouths, fallen trees, docks. Bulls: the mouth of Port Royal Sound, Broad River sandbars, St. Helena Sound, the Fripp and Hunting Island surf and the inlets, often in 20 to 35 ft.
species.tide: Highs well above the average high flood the short grass and the reds tail there. Guides fish from about 2 hours before high, with most of it in the last hour of the incoming and the first of the outgoing. Otherwise low and moving tides on the bars and creek mouths (Beaufort captains on SCDNR's trends page). Bulls feed 1 to 2 hours either side of the turn. Surf bulls are fished about 2 hours either side of low.
species.waterF: No SCDNR number. Guide: once the water is below about 65°F the fiddlers go down and the reds stop tailing. SCDNR says falling water temperature and shorter days cue spawning.
species.notes: SOLID: SC Code 50-5-1705(D) and 50-5-1710: 15 to 23 in total length, 2 per person, 6 per boat (2018 Act 203). No harvest in federal waters. SCDNR asks for 9/0 or larger circle hooks for bulls. GUIDE LORE: the flood-tide heights. One Beaufort guide says 6 to 7 ft is average and 7.5 to 8.5 ft is a flood, about 10 to 15 a month around the new and full moons, and he names no station. Others measure at the Savannah River mouth (7.5 ft and up) or Charleston Harbor (6.0 ft). At NOAA 8667999 (the app's station) the mean high is 7.60 ft and the mean higher high 7.98 ft above MLLW, so those numbers cannot be put on this chart as they are. Fripps Inlet's mean higher high is 6.69 ft and Clarendon Plantation's is 8.60 ft. Every flat floods at its own height.

species.name: Spotted seatrout
species.local: trout, speckled trout, speck, winter trout (the statute's own name)
species.present: Year-round in the estuaries. In winter they gather in deeper channels and holes.
species.peak: Spring (April and May) and fall (October and November). SCDNR's trends page calls October the peak at Edisto, and Beaufort and Hilton Head guides call November high season. They spawn on evenings from April to September (SCDNR). In the May River they call most from May to September, tuned to the moon.
species.where: Grass lines, creek mouths, points, oyster reefs, docks, and holes in the Beaufort, Broad, Coosaw and Morgan rivers. In winter, the deeper holes. The spawning groups gather at night near piers, pilings, bridges, points and holes.
species.tide: Moving water at creek mouths and around ambush points (Beaufort captains). Grass lines on the higher stages in summer, with popping corks.
species.waterF: May River calling ran from 22 to 30°C, 72 to 86°F (Montie et al. 2015). Cold kill: the SCDNR snapshot puts it at the low to mid 40s °F, and SCDNR's 2018 notice said sustained water under 48°F can injure or kill marine animals. A sudden air-temperature drop that chills the shallows is the danger.
species.notes: SOLID: 14 in TL minimum, 10 per day, no gigging from December 1 to the end of February (50-5-1705, 50-5-1710). Winter kills drive the numbers (2001, 2011, 2018). After a kill, SCDNR asks anglers to release fish through the April to September spawn. The buoy read 42.8°F in January 2025, so ask whether a kill year belongs on the page. The May River finding that a warmer spring means earlier and longer calling is peer reviewed (Monczak et al.).

species.name: Southern flounder
species.present: Spring through fall in the estuaries. Adults leave for offshore in late fall, spawn there through the winter and come back in spring (SCDNR). Juveniles stay inside all winter.
species.peak: Spring and fall (guides, and the booking calendar's Apr, Oct and Nov). SCDNR gives no peak. The fall run out to sea follows falling water temperature, roughly October to December.
species.where: Shallow muddy tidal creeks and creek mouths, docks, fallen trees and other structure. Flooded marsh at high tide.
species.tide: SCDNR: they move up the estuary on the rising tide and drop back as it falls, and adults use flooded marsh at high tide. Guides fish creek mouths on the falling tide.
species.waterF: No fishing number. SCDNR says the offshore migration coincides with falling fall water temperatures. The 73°F in the SCDNR snapshot is about the sex of the young, not a fishing cue.
species.notes: SOLID: 16 in TL, 5 per person, 10 per boat (2021 Act 91, made permanent by 2024 Act 224). Numbers are low in SCDNR surveys. A real wind link: SCDNR says flounder larvae need favourable onshore winds to reach the estuaries. That is biology over years, not a reason to fish today.

species.name: Sheepshead
species.present: Year-round. SCDNR calls them non-migratory, but cold moves them off the near shore to the offshore reefs.
species.peak: SCDNR: shallow water in late spring and late fall into early winter, and spawning on nearshore and offshore reefs and wrecks from late winter to early spring (roughly February to April). An Edisto captain on SCDNR's trends page calls October the best bite, once the water is in the mid 70s.
species.where: Pilings, docks, bridges (the Woods Memorial and the Broad River bridges), rocks, the Hunting Island pier on Fripp Inlet, and the nearshore artificial reefs in winter. Juveniles are on oyster reefs and grass beds.
species.tide: Structure at any tide. Guide lore favours slower current at bridges. They also tail on the flats with the reds and black drum on high tides (a Beaufort captain).
species.waterF: No SCDNR number. Distribution is temperature dependent, moving offshore in the cold. The mid-70s fall bite is one captain's word.
species.notes: SOLID: 14 in TL, 10 per person, 30 per boat. Fiddler crabs are the bait. Hard to get to eat on the flats.

species.name: Black drum
species.local: black drum, big uglies (big fish), puppy drum (small)
species.present: Year-round. Most common near shore and on the coast from February to July (SCDNR). Cold may move them to deeper sounds or offshore.
species.peak: Late winter and spring. SCDNR: they spawn in spring and early summer in high-salinity inlets, sounds and coastal rivers. In the May River they call most in February and March and stop by May.
species.where: Sound mouths, deep holes, oyster beds, docks and fallen trees. On the flats with the reds on high tides. A 1990s SC survey named the Port Royal Sound just north of Hilton Head as a possible red and black drum spawning site that was never confirmed.
species.tide: No sourced tide rule. Around structure, and on the flats with tailing reds on the flood (a Beaufort captain).
species.waterF: May River calling ran from 21 to 26°C, 70 to 79°F (Montie et al. 2015). The Gulf and Florida spawning figures (59 to 75°F) come from elsewhere.
species.notes: SOLID: 14 to 27 in TL slot, 5 per day.

species.name: Cobia
species.present: Near shore from April to October (SCDNR). The inshore run in Port Royal Sound and St. Helena Sound starts mid-April, falls off sharply by July, and most fish have left the inshore waters by September. In early April they show first on the coastal artificial reefs (SCDNR Technical Report 89).
species.peak: May and June. Charter logbooks from 1993 to 2000 peaked in May most years and June in the others. SCDNR found cobia eggs and larvae in every sample in May and June, eggs a few hours old far up the Broad River.
species.where: Port Royal Sound and the Broad River (sandbars, tide rips, buoys, the bridge), St. Helena Sound (the Combahee River channel) and Calibogue Sound. Beaufort County was 80 to 85% of the state's cobia catch. Most are sight-cast from boats.
species.tide: Tide rips, color changes, buoys and floating debris in moving water (guides). Spotting them needs light wind and clear water.
species.waterF: SCDNR: the inshore fishery runs April to June when water inside the estuary approaches 68 to 70°F. An SCDNR marine official in 2011: they move into the Broad River at about 69°F. A Beaufort guide says they are thick from 65°F and rising.
species.notes: SOLID: the Southern Cobia Management Zone is all SC waters south of 32°31.0'N (Jeremy Inlet), so Beaufort, Port Royal Sound and Coosaw Point (32.494°N) are inside it. Taking or possessing cobia there is unlawful from May 1 to 31. From June 1 to April 30 the limit is 1 per person and 3 per boat, at 36 in fork length or more. Outside the zone it is 1 and 6. Federal closures also apply (50-5-1713, 2021 Act 15). The peak month is closed to harvest, so a page should never say 'cobia' in May without that. They are a genetically distinct inshore spawning population (SCDNR). GUIDE LORE: the moon phase sets the first inshore wave. Some Port Royal spots have produced less since about 2017.

species.name: Tarpon
species.present: SCDNR: in South Carolina from April, peaking in July and August. Beaufort guides: they trickle in from June, just behind the cobia, and stay until September or October. A Hilton Head captain's latest one was about October 20.
species.peak: July to September (guides). SCDNR: spawning May to August, probably offshore.
species.where: Port Royal, St. Helena and Calibogue sounds, Deveaux Bank, the railroad trestle and the SC 170/171 bridges over the Broad River, the ballast-rock piles in the mouth of Port Royal Sound, and the Woods Memorial Bridge in Beaufort (the scene's swing bridge). Stay with the menhaden (pogy) schools.
species.tide: A guide: the two hours either side of high or low. Another credits the 7-ft-plus swings with how they feed. Current at sandbars, bridges and structure.
species.waterF: Guides (2013): they arrive when the water reaches the mid 70s and leave once it drops below 75°F. SCDNR: they can be cold-stunned and die below 50°F.
species.notes: SOLID: 1 per day, and only one 77 in fork length or longer may be possessed (50-5-1705(E), 2013 Act 72). In practice it is catch and release.

species.name: Spanish mackerel
species.present: April to November (SCDNR). They winter in south Florida.
species.peak: SCDNR: best during the spring and fall migrations, when the schools pass close to shore. Guides add that the bigger fish come in summer. They spawn May to September.
species.where: Beaches, inlets and the nearshore. A school was reported just outside the Fripp Inlet breakers. Mostly high salinity, over 30 ppt (SCDNR), so the sound mouths and the ocean side more than the rivers.
species.tide: Clean, salty green water. Guides favour moving tides at the inlets.
species.waterF: Guides: from the mid 60s. An Edisto captain on SCDNR's trends page: they keep feeding on top until the water falls into the mid 60s.
species.notes: State waters follow the federal limits (SC Code 50-5-2730). Check the current rules rather than printing them.

species.name: King mackerel
species.present: Spring through fall over the shelf. They go north in spring and early summer and south to Florida in fall (SCDNR). They spawn April to September.
species.peak: A spring run (by mid-May in the Carolinas, late April in a warm year) and a fall run (September to November near shore). The dates are from guides, not SCDNR.
species.where: Nearshore reefs and live bottom: the Fripp, Hunting Island and Betsy Ross reefs and the Beaufort 45-ft reef (a federal special management zone). Small kings have been taken trolling inshore of the Fripp reef in 35 ft. Out on the ledges too.
species.tide: SCDNR: they may move inshore on higher tides and in summer.
species.waterF: Guides: ideal about 68 to 72°F, and gone once the water is in the 50s. A North Carolina guide gives above 65°F.
species.notes: State waters follow the federal limits. This is a boat-and-seas fish, so it belongs where the waves go.

species.name: Bluefish
species.present: Spring and fall migrations. NC Sea Grant: abundant off South Carolina by March and April, then North Carolina.
species.peak: Roughly March to May and October to November. These are general Carolina patterns, and no SCDNR or Beaufort source gives the months.
species.where: Inlets, the surf and sound mouths.
species.waterF: NC Sea Grant: best near 68°F, and almost never in water above 84°F or below 50°F.
species.notes: THIN locally: SCDNR has no species page for bluefish, and no Beaufort report names a run. Check the bluefish limits (ASMFC) before printing any.

species.name: Whiting
species.local: whiting (southern kingfish), the most common of SC's three kingfish
species.present: Year-round. Winters in deeper water off shore (SCDNR).
species.peak: SCDNR: inshore catches peak with the late-spring and early-fall migrations. Guides: slow but alive through the winter, and hot again in early spring (March).
species.where: Sandy and sand-mud bottom off the beaches, near inlets and the mouths of the big sounds. One Beaufort trip found plenty on a sandbar at low tide.
species.tide: No sourced rule. Low tide on the bars in one report.
species.waterF: No number. SCDNR says they tolerate a wider temperature and salinity range than the other kingfish.
species.notes: SOLID: spot, whiting and croaker together are limited to 50 a day by hook and line. A family fish: easy, and in any month.

species.name: Tripletail
species.present: Summer into October. Beaufort captains on SCDNR's trends page say some are still around for part of October. No SCDNR month range.
species.peak: Summer (guides). An uncommon catch around Hilton Head.
species.where: Crab-pot floats, channel markers, buoys and floating debris in the sounds, creeks and the ICW. High salinity, near the ocean.
species.tide: Lighter current: a fast tide jerks the float and they leave it. Calm, clear water and the sun at your back to see them (Gulf guides).
species.notes: SOLID: 18 in TL, 3 per person, 9 per boat (2020 Act 119). They hang under exactly the kind of crab-pot float the scene paints in tiger stripes, if Josh wants a quiet nod. The local evidence is thin.

species.name: Sharks
species.local: sharks: Atlantic sharpnose, bonnethead, blacktip, sandbar, finetooth, scalloped hammerhead; spinner, bull and blacknose less often; tiger sharks in the sounds
species.present: Spring to fall in the estuaries (SCDNR).
species.where: Port Royal and St. Helena sounds, the inlets and the beaches. SCDNR found SC's coastal waters a primary nursery for finetooth, blacktip, sandbar, sharpnose and scalloped hammerhead (Ulrich et al. 2007). Its satellite tagging points to the southern sounds as tiger shark foraging and possibly nursing grounds.
species.waterF: SOLID (SCDNR MRRI): they arrive in spring when the water reaches 19 to 20°C (66 to 68°F) and start offshore in fall once it drops below 26°C (79°F).
species.notes: Federal shark rules apply in state waters (SC Code 50-5-2725). Great whites must be released. SCDNR's page says only sharpnose and bonnethead may be kept without the 54 in fork length minimum, but that page may be dated, so do not print regulations.

species.name: White and brown shrimp
species.local: shrimp; roe shrimp (big spring whites); the fall crop; shrimp baiting; cast netting
species.present: White shrimp: the overwintered roe shrimp in spring (the year's biggest), and a fall crop that grows up in the creeks. Brown shrimp: into the estuaries from late February and March, in the creeks from early June, commercially June to August. Fresh local shrimp from May to the end of fall (SCDNR).
species.peak: Fall whites, August to December. Commercial landings start in August and peak in September and October. The baiting season (see shrimp) sits inside it. Commercial trawling opened June 2 in 2025.
species.where: Tidal creeks and rivers. Baiting is on the edges of deeper creeks and channels, mostly at night. SCDNR says to fish closer to the ocean for bigger shrimp.
species.tide: SCDNR: bigger shrimp leave the nurseries on the outgoing tide, mostly at night, and the migration to sea comes on the big tides of the new and full moons.
species.waterF: SCDNR: with little rain, whites stay in the estuaries until the water falls to about 60 to 65°F. In a wet year most go out in August, about a month early. Water at 46°F or colder for 7 days or more kills most of the overwintering brood stock, which cuts the next year's crop.
species.notes: The moon-tide migration is SCDNR's own statement, not almanac. Shrimp baiting is set by statute and SCDNR (see shrimp).

species.name: Dolphin (mahi) and wahoo, offshore
species.local: mahi, dolphin, wahoo, blackfin tuna: the family boater's deep-sea trips
species.present: In the Gulf Stream, roughly 50 to 70 miles out from this part of the coast (charter listings).
species.peak: Charleston-area captains: tuna and wahoo from early March, mahi in big numbers from May well into June, and wahoo again in fall. An Edisto captain on SCDNR's trends page: they feed high in the water column when it reaches about 75°F.
species.where: The Gulf Stream edge and the ledges.
species.tide: Not a tide fish. Wind and seas decide the trip.
species.notes: THIN: only charter and magazine sources, nothing from SCDNR or specific to Beaufort. If anything here, put it with the waves and not the tide.

fish.shrimp:
THE RULE. The statute is SC Code §50-5-1100(B): "The department shall establish annually a sixty-day open season between September 1 and November 15 for taking shrimp over baited areas. The sixty days may but are not required to be consecutive." SCDNR's practice, on its shrimp baiting page and in every release I found, is a season "beginning each year on the last Friday before (or on) September 15". It opens at noon that Friday and closes at noon 60 days later, which is always a Tuesday. The releases match: 2014 opened September 12; 2015 ran September 11 to November 10; 2016 ran September 9 to November 8; 2020 ran September 11 to November 10. For 2026: September 15 is a Tuesday, so the season opened at noon on Friday September 11 and closes at noon on Tuesday November 10, 2026. I worked that out from the rule and the 2020 precedent and did not find SCDNR's own 2026 release. Today, October 16, it is open with 25 days left. Because the statute allows another schedule, a page should hold the year's dates as a constant checked against that September's release, and never assume them in silence.

LIMITS AND GEAR (statute). §50-5-1105(A): 48 quarts of whole shrimp or 29 quarts headed, per set of poles per day, and a day runs sunrise to sunrise. §50-5-1105(B): the same cap on possession on the water from May 1 to December 15. §50-5-1100(F): ten poles per boat a day (ten per person without a boat), each pole no more than an inch thick, with reflective tape and the department's tag. §50-5-1100(C) and (E): a shrimp baiting license with 10 tags, $25 resident and $500 nonresident. Resident helpers in the licensee's boat need no license of their own. Cast nets over bait need at least 1/2 in square or 1 in stretch mesh. In the closed season, having poles or bait material aboard is unlawful. Drop nets from a fixed pier or dock are exempt from the season.

WHERE IT IS PUBLISHED. The SCDNR news release each September (dnr.sc.gov/news), SCDNR's shrimp baiting page (dnr.sc.gov/marine/shrimp), the SC Code (Title 50, Chapter 5, Article 11, at scstatehouse.gov/code/t50c005.php), SCDNR's annual rules guide, and Carolina Sportsman's yearly opening story.

SHRIMP RUNS (SCDNR). There are two crops of white shrimp. The roe shrimp spawn in spring and early summer. Their young enter the creeks in late May and June, grow there two to three months, and are the fall crop. Without much rain the whites stay in the estuaries until the water drops to about 60 to 65°F, then go to sea on the big new and full moon tides. In a wet year most leave in August. Commercial landings start in August and peak in September and October. Seven or more days of water at 46°F or colder kill most of the wintering whites, and the next spring's roe crop with them. Brown shrimp come into the estuaries in late February and March, are cast-netted in the creeks from early June, and are fished commercially June to August. At the Fripp buoy the water averaged 66°F in November and 57.6°F in December over 2023 to 2025. That is the honest whites-going-out cue, measured offshore, where the creeks cool sooner.
fish.calendar:
HOW A PAGE COULD SAY WHAT IS RUNNING, HONESTLY.

1. Keep two kinds of sentence apart, the way the farm keeps "Almanac fishing times" apart from the weather. (a) The calendar: what SCDNR says is in season this month. The family named no species in the Granola talk, so the list is ours to choose, which is a reason to show it rather than score it. This can only ever say "in season", never "running now" or "biting". (b) The measurement: the Fripp buoy's water temperature now (41067, already on the note). Nothing should combine the two into a call. The page can put the reading beside each fish's sourced window and let the family connect them. No bite score, no best fish and no green.

2. The month table. Present and peak months come from SCDNR's species pages, its 2025 snapshots and Technical Report 89 (cobia), and the statutes. Guide months are only filled in where SCDNR is silent (bull reds by month, tarpon's July to September, the flood-tide season). Each entry carries its source. The fixed facts are the law's: cobia closed May 1 to 31 here; the shrimp baiting season (noon Sept 11 to noon Nov 10, 2026); no trout gigging from Dec 1 to the end of February.

3. Water-temperature cues, most trusted first.
- SCDNR's own figures: sharks arrive at 66 to 68°F and start leaving below 79°F. Cobia come inside at 68 to 70°F (about 69 into the Broad). White shrimp leave at 60 to 65°F and die after 7 or more days at 46°F or below. Seatrout winter kills come in the low to mid 40s, and sustained water under 48 is dangerous. Tarpon are cold-stunned below 50.
- Peer-reviewed and local (the USC Beaufort May River recordings): black drum call at 70 to 79°F in February and March, seatrout at 72 to 86°F from May to September, and reds in September and October.
- Guides: tarpon arrive in the mid 70s and leave below 75. Reds stop tailing below about 65 when the fiddlers go down. Spanish feed on top until the mid 60s. Kings like 68 to 72. Sheepshead bite best in the mid 70s.
- Region-wide, not local: bluefish near 68 (NC Sea Grant).
- Buoy 41067's own year, from SECOORA ERDDAP (my own averages of daily means, May 2023 to October 16 2026, every reading QC flag 2): Jan 52.7, Feb 53.0, Mar 59.7, Apr 67.9, May 75.3, Jun 80.4, Jul 85.6, Aug 84.9, Sep 81.1, Oct 73.8, Nov 66.1, Dec 57.6°F. The coldest daily mean was 45.4°F in January 2025. Today it reads 77.2°F (25.08°C at 10:40 UTC), warm for mid-October: October 2026 so far averages 78.4 against 73.8 for the month. The preview's SEA table, [52,53,58,66,74,81,85,86,83,75,65,56], is close to this and could be replaced by it.
- Caveat for every cue: the buoy is 4 nm off Fripp Inlet in the ocean. The shallow creeks warm sooner in spring and cool sooner in fall, and most guide numbers do not say where the water was measured. A threshold should read "the water off Fripp is 69°", never "cobia are in".

4. The tide chart, Beaufort's own, from solid data. NOAA 8667999's datums (epoch 1983 to 2001, accepted 2003), in feet above MLLW: MHW 7.60, MHHW 7.98, mean range 7.39, highest astronomical tide 9.80. A high above MHHW is a big spring-tide high, and the chart could mark it with NOAA's own line. The guides' redfish flood heights (7.5 to 8.5 ft with no station named, 7.5 at the Savannah River mouth, 6.0 at Charleston Harbor) belong to other stations and to particular flats. Fripps Inlet's MHHW is 6.69 and Clarendon Plantation's 8.60, so drawing a "redfish" line at a number would be invented. Wind: guides say an east or northeast wind piles water in and keeps it, and a west wind holds it out. Real, but this station is predictions only with no gauge, so the page cannot measure the wind's effect and must keep saying "by the table". The moon belongs here as SCDNR states it: white shrimp go out on the new and full moon tides, and those are the flood tides. Shrimp baiting is a fact to put on the water section while it is open.

5. Wind, which matters to the family boater and the family pilot. The solid part is about the boat and the water, not the bite: the seas (Open-Meteo, already the note), and the entrance to Port Royal Sound, which turns rough with an onshore wind against the ebb and breaks after a cold front (Waterway Guide), with a cruising club warning about northeast winds. Sight fishing (cobia, tripletail, tailing reds) needs light wind and clear water, which is guide experience that matches common sense. FOLKLORE: "wind from the east, fish bite the least; wind from the west, fish bite the best". The Lowcountry guides contradict it, because they want an east wind for a flood tide.

6. Folklore and soft claims to label or leave out: solunar major and minor times (almanac only, the farm's precedent); the moon phase setting the cobia's first wave (one guide); barometer rules; the booking site's month grid (marketing, and it rates tarpon Great in May); bull reds following the mullet run (plausible lore). Semi-solid: spotted seatrout calling is tied to the moon (May River research), and white shrimp migrate on the spring tides (SCDNR).

7. Which to trust, in order: the SC Code and SCDNR releases; SCDNR's species pages and 2025 snapshots (some pages cite literature from 2009, but agree with the 2025 snapshots); SCDNR technical reports and peer-reviewed Beaufort County work (Montie and Monczak); captains on SCDNR's Saltwater Fishing Trends page (it carries no date and looks like late September 2024); Carolina Sportsman, Gink and Gasoline and charter sites (often a decade old). Regulations change, so a page should not print bag limits. The two date facts, the cobia closure and the shrimp season, are the only law worth showing.

tide.floodTide:
THE NUMBER: 8.0 ft MLLW on NOAA 8667999 (Beaufort, Beaufort River). This is NOAA's own mean higher high water there, rounded: datums pulled live from api.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov (epoch 1983-2001; STND MHHW 11.04, MLLW 3.06, so MHHW is 7.98 ft over MLLW; MHW 7.60; mean range MN 7.39; great diurnal range GT 7.98; HAT 9.80 ft MLLW on 2011-10-27; NAVD88 sits 4.43 ft over MLLW). The station is predictions only: it was established in 1977, removed in 1997, and has floodlevels null. Use about 8.8 ft as 'a big flood' and about 9.8 ft as coastal flooding.

EVIDENCE. Guides rarely say which tide table they mean, so I converted every number onto 8667999. I paired all 705 predicted highs of 2026 against Fort Pulaski 8670870 (Beaufort = 0.941 x FtP + 0.834, rms 0.19 ft, Beaufort about 57 min later) and against Charleston 8665530 (Beaufort = 1.073 x CHS + 1.739, rms 0.22 ft).
- John Holbrook, Beaufort casting instructor (Carolina Sportsman): reds go onto the flats when Savannah River entrance is 7.5 ft or more. That is about 7.9 on 8667999, and 7.5 is exactly Fort Pulaski's own MHHW (7.50).
- LoCo Fly Charters: 'between 7.5 and 8.3 at the Savannah River Entrance', which is 7.9 to 8.6 on 8667999. On 'a really big tide (8.5-9')' you get about 20 minutes on the incoming. That is about 8.8 to 9.3 here.
- Charleston consensus (Carolina Sportsman, Scotty Davis of Lowcountry Fly Shop): 6.0 ft at Charleston Harbor, and 5.8 is nearly the same. That is about 7.96 to 8.18 here. The 'magic six-foot mark' (Charleston Magazine) is the same rule.
- Bay Street Outfitters (Beaufort): 'between 7.8ft and 9ft', no station named.
- Indigo Fishing Charters (Beaufort): ideal 7.6 to 7.8 ft, no station named.
- Owen Plair, Beaufort guide (Gink & Gasoline): average tide '6-7 ft', floods '7.5-8.5 ft', 'around 10-15' a month. His 'average 6-7' fits Fort Pulaski's table (2026 median high 6.97) and not 8667999's (7.42), so his 7.5 to 8.5 is about 7.9 to 8.8 here.
- The counts back this up. Plair's 10 to 15 a month matches 8667999 at 8.0 (12.0 highs a month in 2026), Fort Pulaski at 7.5 (15.2) and Charleston at 5.8 to 6.0 (13.8 / 9.6). At 7.5 on 8667999 it would be 27 a month.
- Physically, Spartina alterniflora grows between MSL and MHHW, and the short high-marsh grass sits near the top of that range (Morris et al., Oceanography 2013). So the grass is wet only on highs over about MHHW, and LoCo wants 'a foot or so of water' over it.
- CAVEAT: the NOAA tables nearest the house are subordinates of Fort Pulaski. Sams Point, Lucy Point Creek 8667733 is 1.1 mi away, at highs x0.97 and +55 min. So an app showing that table reads about 0.6 ft lower than 8667999 for the same water: 8.0 here is about 7.6 at Fort Pulaski and about 7.4 at Sams Point. The chart's line has to be on 8667999's own scale.

HOW OFTEN (NOAA hilo predictions for 2025, 2026 and 2027, lst_ldt):
- Highs of 8.0 or more: 148 / 144 / 157 a year, on 120 / 127 / 135 days. About half fall 7a-7p.
- 8.5 or more: 55 / 60 / 64. Season peaks: 9.69 (2025), 9.36 (2026, Oct 27-28 at about 10-11 am), 9.26 (2027).
- In the guides' season (mid-March to end of November; tailing stops below about 65 F water per Bay Street, Plair and Indigo), days with a daylight high of 8.0 or more number 58 / 67 / 72. For 8.5 or more it is 21 / 26 / 29.
- By month in 2026 (8.0+, daylight, in season): May 1, Jun 2, Jul 3, Aug 9, Sep 18, Oct 21, Nov 13. Fall is the daytime flood season. In April-July the big spring-tide high is the evening or night one (Apr 15-23 2026: 8:26 pm to 2:33 am; Jun 11-19: 6:35 pm to 1:00 am). In Sep-Nov it is the morning one (Oct 24-31: 8:06 am to 1:58 pm; Nov 22-29: 6:34 am to 12:44 pm). This is because high water at Beaufort follows the moon's transit by about 8.3 h, so spring-tide highs land around 8-11 am and pm.
- They are spring tides. Highs of 8.0 or more fall from 2 days before to 4 days after a new or full moon (peak +1 to +2 days); 8.5 or more from -2 to +4.
- For this month: floods Oct 1-14 and Oct 24 to Nov 1, with the next on Oct 24 at 8:06 am, 8.34 ft.

HOURS EITHER SIDE OF HIGH:
- Guides: start about 2 h before high, with most action in the last hour of the flood and the first of the ebb, and tails thinning after about 2 h (Plair). LoCo: 1.5-2 h before to 1.5-2 h after. Bay Street: 2 h either side. Indigo: 2 h either side, about 1 h on small floods, up to 3 h on king tides. Charleston: fish arrive 1-2 h before dead high.
- Measured on 8667999's 6-minute predictions (Sep-Oct 2026), total hours the table stays at or over 8.0 / 7.5 ft: an 8.3 high 1.6 / 2.8; an 8.6 high 2.3 / 3.2; an 8.9 high 2.9 / 3.7; a 9.2 high 3.4 / 4.0. The water rises up to 2.4 ft an hour mid-flood.

TOP END:
- NWS minor flood at Fort Pulaski is 9.5 ft MLLW (station floodlevels: nws_minor 13.00 STND, MLLW 3.50), which is about 9.8 on 8667999, equal to its HAT. That belongs to the alert strip, not the fishing line.

THE TABLE RUNS LOW:
- Fort Pulaski's gauge ran a mean 0.51 ft over its table from Oct 2025 to Sep 2026: +1.02 in Oct 2025, +0.01 in Nov 2025, +0.78 in Sep 2026.
- Guides' numbers are empirical against published tables, so they already absorb this. A live gauge is the honest way to show it. USGS 02176603 'Beaufort River at Beaufort' (32.4274,-80.6693, about 0.4 mi from the NOAA site) reports gage height every 15 min. Its datum is NAVD88 0.00, so MLLW = gage + 4.43, using NOAA's 8667999 datum. It sends CORS *, is provisional, and lands about 30 min late.
- Against 8667999's predictions (Aug 17 to Oct 16 2026): slope 1.02, lag 0, mean departure +0.59 ft (sd 0.58). Oct 10 it peaked at 10.10 vs 8.63 predicted under the coastal flood event. At 6:45 am today it was +0.2 ft.
tide.movingWater:
At the house the turn of the table is the turn of the current, and the steepest part of the curve is the strongest current.
- NOAA current predictions for Oct 2026 at Coosaw River, NE of Sams Point (ACT7161, nearest the house): slack is within 5 to 12 min of 8667999's high and low, max ebb comes 3.1 h after high, max flood 2.6 h after low. The ebb is stronger (median 1.4 kt, max 1.8) than the flood (0.8, max 1.1).
- Port Royal Sound, Middle Shoal (SAV2321): slack 16 to 21 min after the table's turns, max current about 2.9 h after each turn, ebb median 1.7 kt.
- St. Helena Sound, Egg Bank (ACT7111): slack 34 to 41 min before the turns, max ebb 2.4 h after high, ebb median 1.9 kt and max 2.4 against flood 1.2.
- Fripps Inlet (ACT7171): slack about 50 to 57 min before the turns.
- Exception: Beaufort River at the bridge (ACT7231) is predicted to keep flooding about 2 h past the table's high (slack before ebb +126 min) while turning about 21 min after low. A pill there must say high or low water, never 'slack'.

What guides say, as stages a pill can name from time to the table's turn:
(1) Flood-tide tailing: the last of the flood into the first of the ebb, about 2 h either side of a high of 8.0 or more (Plair, LoCo, Bay Street, Indigo).
(2) Low-water reds: 'Redfish should bite better and better on low and moving tides' (SCDNR Saltwater Fishing Trends, Beaufort, October 2026, Capts. Tuck Scott and Patrick Kelly). The falling tide drains the grass and pushes fish into creeks and onto mud flats (Tuck Scott, Carolina Sportsman). Airport Flats are fished 'on a low and rising tide' (Capt. Richard Sykes, Bay Street). In Charleston: 'the last part of the outgoing through the slack tide and the first part of the incoming' (David Yates), and the first 2 h of the incoming (Charleston Insider).
(3) Dead water: the bite was 'wide open for more than an hour' on the falling tide and quit when the 'tide stopped running' (Trea Everett, Barrier Island Marine, Beaufort, Carolina Sportsman).
(4) Trout: 'Trout will be caught around the mouths of creeks in moving water' (SCDNR Oct 2026). 'From half-tide rising until about an hour after high' (Sykes). Danny Rourk (Tailwind Charters) finds the incoming better at most Beaufort River spots, but 'any kind of moving water' works.
(5) In November and winter, reds don't feed at high tide, so low-tide flats are best (Carolina Sportsman 'High Water Mark').

Stage words a chart could draw, all with the table's high and low as the turn: 'first of the flood' (0-2 h after low), 'last of the flood' (2 h before high), 'high water' (within 30 min), 'first of the ebb' (0-2 h after high), 'last of the ebb' (2 h before low), 'low water'. The strongest current is mid-tide, about 3 h after each turn.
tide.windTide:
WIND MOVES THE FLOOD (this is the wind that matters for fishing).
Bay Street Outfitters says a west wind holds water out and can rule a flood out, while an east wind pushes water in so a smaller tide fishes. Indigo says some winds hold water on the flats and others blow it out. Capt. Jamie Hough (Georgia Bight, Salt Water Sportsman) says a northeast wind will 'push the water in and hold it in'. Carolina Sportsman (Mark Dickson): 'Three or four inches of extra water can make all the difference in the world.'

Measured at NOAA Fort Pulaski (8670870, which has a wind sensor), Oct 2025 to Sep 2026: departure from the table against its typical +0.45 ft, by the 12-hour mean wind in knots.
- NE: 8-13 kt +0.60, 13-18 kt +0.99, 18+ kt +1.29 ft.
- E: 8-13 kt +0.45, 13-18 kt +0.92, 18+ kt +1.24 ft.
- S, SE, SW: about 0 to -0.2 ft.
- W: 8-13 kt -0.53 ft.
- NW: 8-13 kt -0.30, 13-18 kt -0.62, 18+ kt -0.99 ft.
So a day of 15-20 mph NE or E adds about a foot, enough to flood the grass on a 7.0 ft table high. A NW blow of the same strength takes off half a foot to a foot and can leave an 8.5 dry. The honest way to draw it is the measured gap, from the USGS Beaufort River gauge (02176603), never a forecast setup.

WIND AGAINST TIDE IN THE SOUNDS AND INLETS.
The ebb sets out to the southeast and the flood back to the northwest. NOAA ebb and flood directions: Port Royal Sound Middle Shoal 160 and 335 degrees, St. Helena Sound Egg Bank 128 and 329, Fripps Inlet 104 and 299, Coosaw near Sams Point 117 and 292. So winds from about E through S oppose the ebb, and winds from about W through N oppose the flood.
- Coast Pilot 4 ch. 7 (11 Oct 2026 edition), Port Royal Sound: currents 1.5 kt on the bar, 1.8 off Hilton Head, 1.4 at the Beaufort River entrance, 2 kt or more in the sound. 'Winds greatly influence the velocity of the tidal current, especially on the runout after prolonged easterlies, which on the ebb often reaches 5 knots.' On the ebb at the turn into Bay Point Reach a strong current sets across toward St. Michaels Breakers. On the flood the current 'sets directly onto the shoals', and Fishing Rip's tide rips can look like breakers. Breaking shoals run about 10 mi off Bay Point and 8 mi off Hilton Head.
- Coast Pilot, St. Helena Sound: a 7-mile entrance with shoals about 6 mi seaward, depths up to 14 ft less than charted, entrance currents about 2 kt, mean range about 6 ft on the bar. Fripp Inlet is 'well defined by breakers' and 'subject to continual change', so local knowledge only. Trenchards Inlet had a 3 ft controlling depth (1983). Prevailing winds are NE in fall and winter and S in spring and summer, averaging about 10 kt.
- Waterway Guide (boater alert, Port Royal Sound entrance): a stiff onshore breeze against an ebb is 'best avoided', and after a cold front expect breaking swells through the channel until Bay Point. A 26-ft boat found a southerly against the ebb from Skull Creek into the Beaufort River rough with whitecaps and anchored to wait.
- Rule of thumb, not official: each knot of opposing current acts like about 10 kt of extra wind (Waggoner, as quoted on TrawlerForum).

WIND LIMITS FOR SMALL BOATS.
- No published NWS Charleston criteria found. The authoritative line is a Small Craft Advisory in marine zone AMZ362 (Coastal waters from Edisto Beach SC to Savannah GA out 20 NM) or AMZ382 (20-60 NM), read from api.weather.gov. CHS advisories in practice run at 15-25 kt gusting 30, with seas 3-8 ft. None was active Oct 16 2026.
- The app's existing boat lines (gusts 22 / 30 mph, seas 3 / 5 ft, `boatSay`) are Josh's and can be reused. Do not invent new ones.
- Measured seas: buoy 41067 (the one already read for water temperature) also reports significant wave height, period and direction hourly on SECOORA ERDDAP. At 10:40 UTC today it read 0.45 m (1.5 ft) at 4.2 s with water 25.1 C. That is a measurement to set beside Open-Meteo's model for the family boater's trips past the bars.

SIGHT FISHING AND WIND.
- No SC source gives a mph cutoff. Lowcountry guidance: 'Early mornings with light winds are usually best' (Charleston Magazine). Chop on the flats made reds hard to see in a 25 mph SE wind behind Bulls Bay (Rob Beglin, Carolina Sportsman). Plair picks leader length by wind and sky, and on clear days you can see the fish's body. A Texas guide calls under 10 mph ideal and 15+ by 9 am hard (not local).
- So the chart can print the wind over the flood window but should not grade sight fishing by it.
tide.solunar:
Solunar times do not belong on Beaufort's tide chart. Here they are the tide by another name.

High water at Beaufort follows the moon's transit by a nearly fixed interval. NOAA's Greenwich high water interval for 8667999 is 1.65 h, about 8.5 h local. Checked against USNO moon data for Sep 1 to Oct 30 2026 and 8667999's predictions (local standard time):
- Every moon transit, the centre of an almanac 'major', fell on the falling tide: 115 of 115, a median 4.1 h after high (IQR 3.8-4.4) and 2.1 h before low (IQR 1.9-2.2).
- Every moonrise and moonset, the centre of a 'minor', fell on the rising tide: 116 of 116, a median 2.4 h before high (IQR 2.9-1.1 h before).
- The farm's windows are transit plus or minus 60 min and rise/set plus or minus 30 min (`solunarWindows`). Drawn at Beaufort, majors would always shade the middle and late ebb, ending about 1 h before low, and minors the late flood. That is the same thing the tide curve and the guides' stage rules already say, under a second theory with its own label.

How guides treat it. None of the Beaufort or Lowcountry guides or reports found mention solunar tables. They talk tide stage, tide height and moving water. The SCDNR monthly trends do, Carolina Sportsman does, and Plair says moon phase matters only because it sets how many floods there are. The moon's honest role here is the spring tide: flood tides of 8.0 ft or more cluster from 2 days before to 4 days after new and full moon, and Charleston Magazine says to look for tailing tides 'around the full and new moons'. The science is weak and species-specific. NOAA Fisheries' Pulver (N. Am. J. Fish. Mgmt. 2017) found a lunar-cycle effect on Gulf reef-fish catch rates for red grouper and tilefish, none for red snapper, vermilion snapper or yellowedge grouper. Other studies cited there found effects of a few percent.

Recommendation: keep 'Almanac fishing times' a farm feature, since a pond has no tide. At Beaufort, let the moon show up as the cause of the flood tides (the phase in the note, or the spring-tide days), never as a second set of times.
rules: GRASS LINE: draw a horizontal line across Beaufort's tide chart at 8.0 ft MLLW. That is NOAA 8667999's own MHHW of 7.98, so the chart's honest 0-from-MLLW scale carries it with no new scale. A predicted high at or over it is a flood tide: the table puts water over the short spartina. Source: NOAA datums (live), with guide numbers converted onto 8667999: Fort Pulaski 7.5 (Holbrook / Carolina Sportsman; LoCo Fly 7.5-8.3), Charleston 5.8-6.0 (Carolina Sportsman / Lowcountry Fly Shop), Bay Street Outfitters 7.8-9, Plair 7.5-8.5 on a Fort Pulaski-like table. All land at about 7.9-8.2. Plair's '10-15 a month' matches 8667999 at 8.0 (12 a month in 2026). This is a fact about water, so it can be drawn every day of the year.

FLOOD BAND: shade the hours the table is at or over 8.0 ft around each such high, a wash of the hours, not a score. On 8667999 that is about 1.6 h for an 8.3 high, 2.3 h for 8.6, 2.9 h for 8.9 and 3.4 h for 9.2 (NOAA 6-minute predictions). Guides fish from about 2 h before to 2 h after (Plair, LoCo Fly, Bay Street Outfitters, Indigo), so the band plus or minus 30-45 min is where they say fish arrive.

SEASON WORD: say 'flood tide' / 'tailing' only mid-March to the end of November (Bay Street Outfitters, Plair, Indigo: 'mid-March through Thanksgiving'). The fiddlers go down and reds stop tailing below about 65 F water (64-65 F in Bay Street, Plair, Indigo). Buoy 41067's thermometer is offshore (4 nm SE of Fripp), so use it only to explain, never to certify the marsh. Outside the season the line and band stay, because the water is still in the grass, but the word goes.

BIG FLOOD: at or over about 8.8 ft on 8667999 (LoCo's 8.5-9 at Fort Pulaski, where 'you get about 20 minutes of fishing' on the incoming before it is too deep) the band can say the grass is deep. At or over about 9.8 ft (Fort Pulaski NWS minor flood 9.5 ft MLLW converted, equal to 8667999's HAT 9.80) it is coastal flooding, and that is the alert strip's to say, not the fishing chart's.

MEASURED GAP, NOT A WIND FORECAST: put the existing level tag beside the skiff (`levelFeet` / `levelGap`) on USGS 02176603 Beaufort River at Beaufort. Gage height is on NAVD88 0, so MLLW = gage + 4.43 by NOAA 8667999's datums. It runs every 15 min, CORS *, provisional, about 30 min late, so it needs a freshness window like `BUOY_FRESH` rather than the half hour Wrightsville's gauge gets. Verified: slope 1.02, lag 0, mean +0.59 ft over Aug 17 to Oct 16 2026, +1.5 ft on Oct 10. When the gap is positive the grass floods on a lower table high, and the sentence says so with the measured number. The curve stays the table's.

WIND THAT FILLS OR EMPTIES THE MARSH: NE or E wind raises the flood and W or NW lowers it (Bay Street Outfitters; Jamie Hough in Salt Water Sportsman; Carolina Sportsman). NOAA Fort Pulaski gauge and wind, Oct 2025 to Sep 2026, 12-h mean wind: NE/E 13-18 kt about +0.9 to +1.0 ft, 18+ kt about +1.25 ft; W 8-13 kt -0.5 ft; NW 13-18 kt -0.6 ft, 18+ kt -1.0 ft; S/SE about 0. A pill can name the wind beside a flood high, but the honest number is the measured gap from the rule above.

WIND AGAINST THE EBB: on the hours the table is falling (high to low), a forecast wind from about E through S (roughly 90-200 degrees) opposes the ebb. That ebb sets out SE at 104-160 degrees in Fripps Inlet, St. Helena Sound and Port Royal Sound (NOAA current predictions), and is strongest about 2.4-3.1 h after high. A wind from about W through N opposes the flood, strongest about 2.6-2.9 h after low. Coast Pilot 4: the ebb runout after prolonged easterlies often reaches 5 kt at Port Royal Sound, and the flood sets onto the shoals. Waterway Guide: a stiff onshore breeze against the ebb is best avoided. Use the app's existing caution line (gusts 22 mph) as the speed rather than inventing one; about 15 mph sustained is where Fort Pulaski's water measurably responds. Draw it as a fact about the hours ('wind against the ebb'), never a grade.

TIDE STAGE WORDS IN THE PILL: name the stage from time to the table's turn: first of the flood (0-2 h after low), last of the flood (2 h before high), high water / low water (within 30 min), first of the ebb (0-2 h after high), last of the ebb (2 h before low). Near the house slack is within 5-21 min of the table's turns (Coosaw River ACT7161, Port Royal Sound SAV2321), but at the Beaufort River bridge (ACT7231) the flood runs about 2 h past high. So never print 'slack', only high or low water. Guides' moving-water rules: reds 'on low and moving tides' and trout 'in moving water' (SCDNR Oct 2026); the bite stops when the 'tide stopped running' (Barrier Island Marine).

MOON AS CAUSE, NOT CLOCK: no almanac windows on Beaufort's tide chart. At Beaufort every moon transit (majors) fell on the ebb, a median 4.1 h after high, and every moonrise and moonset (minors) on the flood, a median 2.4 h before high (USNO plus NOAA, Sep-Oct 2026, 115 and 116 of 116), so they would duplicate the tide. The moon's real effect is the spring tide: 8.0 ft floods fall from 2 days before to 4 days after new or full moon. The phase may ride in the note.

SMALL-BOAT LIMITS: use the app's existing `boatSay` lines (gusts 22 / 30 mph, seas 3 / 5 ft) and the NWS Small Craft Advisory for AMZ362 (Edisto Beach to Savannah out 20 NM) or AMZ382 (20-60 NM) from api.weather.gov. Show buoy 41067's measured significant wave height (hourly on SECOORA ERDDAP, 0.45 m / 4.2 s at 10:40 UTC Oct 16) beside the Open-Meteo marine model for seas past the bars. Invent no new threshold. CHS's own written SCA criteria were not found.

STATION HONESTY: the chart's thresholds must be stated on 8667999. The house's nearest NOAA table (Sams Point, Lucy Point Creek 8667733, 1.1 mi, highs = 0.97 x Fort Pulaski +55 min) reads about 0.6 ft lower for the same water: 8.0 here is about 7.6 at Fort Pulaski, about 7.4 at Sams Point and about 5.84 at Charleston. So never quote a guide's bare number on this chart.

FISH RUN (Jen's ask), out of the tide chart: SCDNR's monthly Saltwater Fishing Trends has a Beaufort inshore section from Capts. Tuck Scott and Patrick Kelly (Bay Street Outfitters). October 2026 covers reds on low and moving tides and tailing on very high tides, trout at creek mouths in moving water, flounder, tripletail, black drum, sheepshead, and bull reds arriving in the inlets. **For boating, on the tide chart (Beaufort's own part):**
- Show a row of hourly wind on the tide chart's own time axis, from Open-Meteo at LOCS.bft (add `wind_direction_10m` to `hourly`).

- No score, no "good fishing" or "go" word, and no "wind against the tide" verdict. That needs the channel's direction and current predictions this station does not give. The vanes over the rising and falling curve let a fisherman see it.
- Gusts from 28 can take the hourly chart's windy treatment (WINDY_GUST).

**For going outside (the family boater):**
- Fetch `alerts/active?zone=AMZ362` and name a Small Craft Advisory, Gale Watch/Warning or Storm Warning in the water section's note or on a card. This is the forecaster's call, and it is the honest gate. Do not put it on the house's strip, which is Jen's too.

- Seas: keep the model for the hours ahead, but know it runs low in a blow (Sunday 5.5 ft against NWS's 8–10). Consider 41067's measured wave height for "now": one more column in the request the page already makes.
- Buoy 41033's measured wind is honest as "off Fripp now" but optional. It is 20 miles out, at 3 m, and up to 70 minutes old. Never mix it into the forecast row.

- At most one quiet line: KNBC's latest METAR wind as a pilot reads it, in knots with direction and gust and its own time (`MCAS Beaufort 230° 9 kt G18 · 6:56a`, `calm`), read from IEM's currents (fresh, CORS *).
- api.weather.gov works as a fallback, about 30 minutes behind.
- Hide it once it is about 90 minutes old.
- Keep it off the tide chart: it is the airfield's reading, not the river's.

- KARW entirely: nothing since Sept 18 2025. Never label anything KARW.
- KNBC's TAF: no browser-readable source, and none is issued on weekends or holidays.
- Open-Meteo presented as an aviation forecast.
- Flight-category colours, crosswind, density altitude.
- The coastal waters forecast presented as the river's (AMZ362 is the ocean out 20 nm).
- Open-Meteo's sea-cell gusts.
- The ERDDAP KNBC mirror (too slow).
- Anything fetched straight from aviationweather.gov, tgftp or NDBC realtime2: a phone browser cannot read them (no CORS).

verdict.summary:
I rank C first, A a close second and B third. All three branches pass test.mjs (74 of 74). I read every screenshot in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-workmac-Documents-Codex-2026-08-03-github-plugin-github-openai-curated-remote-work-porch-weather-oak-preview/b29199e6-b38b-4565-b71f-78d5b8b7339b/scratchpad/mocks/ and each branch's index.html diff against main. Gzipped size goes from 404 KB on main to 412–417 KB.

C ranks first because it is the only option that answers everything Josh asked for: the flood tide (the honest fishing time here, since solunar times would only repeat the tide), what's in season, and the wind. It also adds the offshore advisory for the family boater. The flood tide is a green 8 ft gridline with a spartina tuft and 'flood tide' printed once over the first flood high. The flood words are judged on each stop's own water level. The wind row starts at now with the chip's own reading, and the data is real (NOAA predictions, plus the real Open-Meteo run and buoy for today). Its problems are mostly things to take away:
- Reds are missing from the calendar from March to July, under a 'flood tide' label that C itself ties to tailing reds.
- Gusts, the pill's wind and the advisory are coloured red, against 'no reading is coloured'.
- The wind row has too much text: up to 9 arrows plus a second row of 'g15' gusts.
- The advisory for zone AMZ362 doesn't say it is the ocean offshore, not the river.
- The advisory fetch can hold the paint up to 6 seconds.
- The moving-water streaks are weak, and the shrimp is pink like a cooked one.

A is the most restrained and best crafted. Its green flood wash with grass standing in the water, its season check per high and its larger fish row (cobia 'closed' in May, shrimp 'baiting') are the best of the three. But the wind, which Josh called very important, only appears when you touch the chart. The pill also says 'deep in the grass' at 8.0 ft, because it uses the high's category instead of the level at that stop. It uses font glyphs for the wind arrows, and its chevrons repeat what the slope of the curve already shows.

B has the best-drawn wind (a line with a gust wash on one fixed scale, using the chip's own arrow) and a sound airfield source. But it skips the fishing half of the ask entirely: no flood tide, no fish. It draws a 'wind against the tide' chop that belongs to the sounds onto the river's tide line, adds a line of airfield text under the chart, and uses made-up tide heights.

The best version to show Josh is C's structure with A's restraint and art, wind in B's quiet style, no red, and the reds fixed.

options.description:
Option C, "The fishing day", revised from the judge's review. Beaufort's water section is still one section with one title and one note ("Water · Beaufort River", "77° · seas ~1 ft"). Its chart does three things Wilmington's doesn't, and none of them is a score.

1. The grass line. A thin green line at 8 ft with a small spartina tuft and "8 ft" beside it. That's NOAA's own average higher high water at the Beaufort station, where the short marsh grass stands. When a high tops it:
   - the hours it stays over the line are washed pale green, starting just under the high's time and never through it;
   - the water above the line turns green and the high's time prints in green;
   - "flood tide" goes over the first one, but only from mid-March to the end of November, judged on that high's own date.
   On a neap day the highs fall short and you can see there's no flood. Real 2026 tides: Oct 10's 10:06a, Oct 27's 9.35 ft king tide at 10:17a, and May 16's 9:39p spring flood. At 320 the "8 ft" now stays: over the line, under it, or a size smaller, before it would ever drop to the tuft alone.

2. The wind row, under the low-tide times. The arrow points into the wind, the same arrow as the header chip. There is one number per column, at now and at each high and low still ahead, about six hours apart. So you can read the wind at the flood high or at the morning low. "mph" is said once on now's column where there's room. The "g22" gust row and all the red are gone. Gusts are in the chip and the slider, in the chip's own words ("↑ 20, gusts 29 mph"). When the coastal waters have a Small Craft Advisory or Gale Watch, a grey bar runs over its hours, labelled "offshore small craft advisory · gale watch", because that zone is the ocean, not the river. It never goes on the house's alert strip.

3. Under the chart, "IN SEASON": little Storybook fish, each about 32 px nose to tail, with their names. They come from SCDNR's calendar for the month:
   - reds every month, called bull reds August to November;
   - October: bull reds, trout, flounder, sheepshead, shrimp (the shrimp is now a pale, raw white shrimp);
   - April and May: reds, trout, flounder, sheepshead, black drum, cobia, with "closed" under cobia in May;
   - January: reds, sheepshead.
   It says "in season", never "biting". Its space is held from the first frame, so nothing jumps when the fish land.

The slider at every stop says the time, the depth, the stage of the water ("first of the incoming", "high water" and so on, never "slack"), "flood tide" or "big flood tide" in green, and the wind with its arrow. Screen readers hear the same words.

Taken out, and why:
- The moving-water streaks: the slope of the curve already is the current, and the slider names the stage.
- Almanac fishing times: at Beaufort every moon-overhead time lands on the falling tide and every moonrise on the rising tide, so they would just repeat the tide.
- The MCAS Beaufort airfield wind: it's the airfield's reading, not the river's.

Porters Neck's water section is unchanged. Its chart markup matches the base apart from one hidden empty element and two numbers 0.1 px apart, the same jitter you get running unchanged code twice.

Checks run:
- 74 of 74 tests pass, in Eastern time and in UTC.
- The Beaufort scene harness is clean for 8 water cases at 320, 390, 430 and 760. It now also checks every month's in-season row: no wraps, never taller than the space held for it.
- tools/interactions.mjs passes 62 scenarios, including 4 new Beaufort ones: every stop read at 320, 390 and 900, and a real finger slide.
- tools/shots.mjs passes.
- tools/webkit.mjs on a new beaufort-afternoon case: 56.8 fps idle and 51.2 opening, against 55.2 and 47.8 on the base page.

REAL (live in the code path, real in the renders):
- Tide: NOAA 8667999's real 2026 high/low table (MLLW, local time), in tools/beaufort/fixtures/tides-8667999-2026.json. Every water case runs on it, including:
  - king-tide: Oct 27, 9.35 ft at 10:17a;
  - water-night: Oct 23;
  - the new may-evening case: May 16, the 9.12 ft spring flood at 9:39p.
- Grass line, 8 ft: NOAA's own mean higher high water at the station (MHHW 7.98), rounded. The flood bands are worked out from the table.
- Stage words: worked out from the table's turns ("high water" or "low water" within 30 minutes of one, "first of" or "last of" within 2 hours, never "slack").
- Wind: the app asks Open-Meteo for hourly wind_direction_10m at every place, but only Beaufort draws it. The row's columns fall at now and at the table's own turns.
- "today" case: the real Open-Meteo run at the house (fetched 7 am Oct 16), the real Fripp buoy reading of 77.2°F, and Open-Meteo marine's 1.3 ft of seas.
- Marine zone AMZ362 is fetched on its own lane (alerts/active?zone=AMZ362) and never on the house's strip.
- What changed in the code path this round:
  - the zone request no longer holds the forecast's paint; a late answer repaints only when it changes what the row shows;
  - the in-season row is a static element, with its height held in the preload, the shell and a cached place switch;
  - sw.js CACHE is now v101.

HARD-CODED / MOCK:
- Marine advisories:
  - the windy-clear Small Craft Advisory is made up, in the alerts API's shape;
  - today's SCA (Sat 5a–2p) and Gale Watch (Sat 2p–Tue 3a) are the times a researcher saw posted, re-typed; they are not the archived products.
- Wind curves in the named cases (sea breeze, a front's veer, May's sea breeze laying down) are synthetic fixture options.
- Buoy temperatures in the named cases are buoy 41067's monthly means from the research; May is 75.3.
- The in-season calendar (RUNS.bft) is my reading of SCDNR's species pages, its snapshots, Technical Report 89 and MRRI:
  - reds all year (SCDNR: year-round), bull reds Aug–Nov (SCDNR spawning run, plus guides);
  - sharks trimmed to Jun–Sep so April and May fit one row at 320;
  - the cobia May closure is SC Code 50-5-1713.
  It all needs an SCDNR check before shipping.
- Shrimp-baiting dates are still left out: the 2026 dates are derived, not confirmed by SCDNR's release.
- The fish drawings are new. The white shrimp is option A's drawing, ported.
- AGENTS.md is not updated (mock branch); it needs a section if this ships.

NOT BUILT (next step to offer Josh): the USGS 02176603 Beaufort River gauge. Gage height + 4.43 = MLLW, it allows browser requests, and it ran +0.59 ft over the table on average (Aug 17 to Oct 16 2026). It would let the existing level tag beside the skiff work here and catch floods the table under-reports.
